title: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
hook: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat, the prayer in its set shape, five times a day. Your line was the body prays too. Did you change your posture at a hard moment? Day fifteen.

Before dawn, in a city still dark, one voice starts up from a minaret. A single voice, rising, holding a note longer than seems possible, then falling away. Then a second voice, farther off, a beat behind. Then another. For a few minutes the rooftops are full of the same words, never quite in sync. It isn't a song, exactly, and it isn't an alarm. It's an invitation, sent out at each of the five prayer times. Today: the call, and what it's actually saying.
screen: `ONE VOICE, HOLDING A NOTE.` → `THEN ANOTHER, A BEAT BEHIND.` → `WHAT IS IT SAYING?`

segments.voice: The adhan. The root, a-dh-n, is the root of the ear, udhun. The call is literally the thing you hear. In the first years in Medina, the hadith collections say, the young community didn't have one. People gathered by guessing the time. The companions talked it over: a bell, like the Christians? A horn, like the Jews? A fire? Then, in a report in Abu Dawud, a companion named Abdullah ibn Zayd dreamed of a man teaching him the words. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said it was a true dream, and told him: teach it to Bilal, his voice carries. Bilal ibn Rabah had been enslaved in Mecca and tortured for his faith: he is the man you met on day ten, saying ahad, one, under the rock. He had since been freed, and now his voice called the city to prayer. Now, the words. Allahu akbar: God is greater. Four times, in Abu Dawud's report. Then two witnesses: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Then the heart of it. Hayya 'ala s-salah: come to prayer. Hayya 'ala l-falah: come to success. Falah is flourishing, and its root is the root of the farmer, the one who splits the ground so something can grow. At dawn, Sunni callers add a line: prayer is better than sleep. The Shia call carries a line of its own at every prayer: come to the best of deeds. A hadith in Abu Dawud tells of the Prophet saying the adhan into the ear of his newborn grandson, al-Hasan, and families still do it, so the first words a child hears are a call. That's why it's beautiful even without the Arabic. Its whole job is to turn toward you and say: come. You, specifically. Now.
screen: `ADHAN — FROM THE ROOT FOR EAR.` · `A DREAM, AND BILAL'S VOICE.` · `COME TO PRAYER. COME TO SUCCESS.` · `SAID INTO A NEWBORN'S EAR.` · then, large: `HAYYA 'ALA L-FALAH.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Close your eyes and listen. Not to anything in particular. Just to what's calling right now. A car outside, the fridge, your own breathing, someone's voice in another room. Each one is asking for a little of your attention. Notice what you turn toward. If you pray, you can let the old words sit under the sound: come to prayer, come to success. The bell holds the time.
The adhan. The call to prayer, from the root for ear. God is greater; come to prayer; come to success. Fifteenth word.
Your line: you are being called. Today, when your phone buzzes or someone says your name, pause for one breath before you answer, and ask what's really calling you. Day fifteen.

howItsDone: In Muslim-majority places a mu'adhdhin gives the adhan from the mosque, often by loudspeaker, at each of the five prayer times; elsewhere it's often heard from an app, and it's said softly into a newborn's ear.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 499 (Abdullah ibn Zayd's dream; 'teach it to Bilal')

notes: The adhan's words are given in transliteration and English paraphrase, not from a published translation. The Sunni form (Allahu akbar four times, two testimonies twice each, hayya 'ala twice each, Allahu akbar twice, la ilaha illallah once) is implied; Maliki practice gives the opening takbir twice. The script says 'four times'; confirm.
Shia adhan: adds 'hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal' and many add a testimony about 'Ali (not considered part of the obligatory adhan by most Shia jurists). The script mentions only the first. Confirm.
'Like the Christians / like the Jews' paraphrases Bukhari 604 and the Abu Dawud report (bell, horn). It's reported speech from the hadith, not a comparison; confirm tone.
Adhan in the newborn's ear: the hadith (Abu Dawud 5105, Tirmidhi 1514) is graded weak by some scholars; the practice is widespread. The script says 'many Muslim families'. Confirm.
Falah and fallah (farmer) sharing the root f-l-h (to split, cleave the soil): confirm.
